newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Chirac says only PLO state gives Israel security.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says only PLO state gives Israel security.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, taking Europe's drive for a Middle East peacemaking role to a reluctant Israel, told young Israelis on Monday that only a Palestinian state could guarantee them real security.

In a policy speech to technology students in the northern city of Haifa, Chirac said: "A recognised Palestinian state will provide Israel with a true partner. Only such a partner will be capable of making, and adhering to the commitments that are necessary for the security of Israel."

But he omitted a call in his prepared text for the European Union to "co-sponsor" the peace process -- the term he used in Syria on Saturday. Instead he said the EU could not be content with being the main aid donor and must make an ever greater political contribution.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu won election in May on a platform pledging "peace with security" but rejecting any further territorial concession to the Arabs and branding a Palestinian state a mortal danger to Israel.

Chirac, who arrived from Syria where he received a hero's welcome, said that a Palestinian state, and a balanced agreement on the status of Jerusalem, the fate of Palestinian refugees and the future of Jewish settlements was "the price of security".

France's backing for a Palestinian state is a longstanding position. But Chirac's blunt statement to an Israeli audience that any peace will be illusory until Israel conceded the PLO's main demand, highlighted why the Netanyahu government argues that neither Paris nor the EU can be honest brokers.

The French leader came to Israel on the day that U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross said he was going home after failing to get Israel and the PLO to agree the terms of a long overdue Israeli troop withdrawal from the West Bank city of Hebron.

While he praised Netanyahu for talking to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Chirac implicitly criticised Israeli foot-dragging on Hebron, saying "agreements entered into must be completely implemented". Otherwise there would be no peace, and thus no security, he said.
He said seven hours of private talks with President Hafez al-Assad had convinced him Syria had opted for peace. "And yet in Syria, as in Israel, there is still deep suspicion."

Peace with Syria meant returning the occupied Golan Heights in exchange for full recognition, security guarantees and normal relations, he said, adding: "The Lebanese problem cannot be solved independently of the other parts of the peace process."

Chirac hinted at potential EU pressure, reminding Israel that its 1995 association agreement with the 15-nation Union, its biggest trading partner, had yet to be ratified by member parliaments. The accord offers Israel far-reaching trade advantages and scientific cooperation.
His visit was preceded by a spate of diplomatic clashes that bared raw feelings on both sides about France's "Arab policy" and Israel's rejection of the "land for peace" principle.

The English-language Jerusalem Post, which often reflects government thinking, branded Chirac in a vitriolic editorial a "biased would-be broker" who showed "fawning support of the region's most unregenerate terrorist states".
Chirac declared himself a friend of Israel, praised the Jewish state's "creative genius" and said France was fully commited to its security.
But even before he reached Jerusalem, Netanyahu had brushed aside France's call for a political role for the European Union, the main aid donor to the region, in Arab-Israeli negotiations.

President Ezer Weizman referred to Israel's claim to sovereignty over all of Greater Jerusalem, not recognised by most of the international community, when he welcomed Chirac to "Jerusalem, eternal capital of the state of Israel".

While Chirac reviewed an honour guard with Weizman, his junior health minister, Herve Gaymard, was visiting a disputed PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem to meet Palestinian minister Faisal al-Husseini.

France decided its foreign minister would boycott the Israel leg of Chirac's trip after the Israelis refused to let him visit Orient House, which the Netanyahu administration says violates Israel-PLO peace accords.
